owners.title: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One

candidates.solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{2x} & <\frac{1}{3} \\ {8}^{2x} & <\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the logarithm to base $8$ of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{2x}) & <{log}_{8}⁡\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ 2x & <{log}_{8}⁡({6}^{-1}) \\ 2x & <-{log}_{8}⁡(6) \\ x & <-\frac{1}{2}{log}_{8}⁡(6).\end{aligned}
$$

candidates.solution:
We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}-2{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's calculate the indefinite integral first. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{x-3}-2\int \frac{\text{d}x}{2x+1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-3}{2x+1}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the improper integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{7}{2{x}^{2}-5x-3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-3}{2x+1}|]}_{4}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{a-3}{2a+1}|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1}{9}|) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{1-\frac{3}{a}}{2+\frac{1}{a}}|)-\operatorname{ln}⁡{9}^{-1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡9 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{9}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

owners.title: Calculating the Average Rate of Change Over a Varying Interval where the Parameter Represents Distance

candidates.solution:
We have the function $f(x)=5sin⁡(2x).$ Notice that we are given the length $h$ of the interval. So, the average rate of change of $f$ over this interval is given by

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

with $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Substituting into the formula and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \\  & =\frac{f(\frac{\pi }{2}+h)-f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{h} \\  & =\frac{5sin⁡(2(\frac{\pi }{2}+h))-5sin⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})}{h} \\  & =\frac{5sin⁡(\pi +2h)-5sin⁡(\pi )}{h} \\  & =\frac{5sin⁡(\pi +2h)-5(0)}{h} \\  & =\frac{5sin⁡(\pi +2h)}{h} \\  & =\frac{5}{h}sin⁡(\pi +2h).\end{aligned}
$$

owners.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

candidates.solution:
In part 3, we saw that the derivative of a particle's velocity with respect to time gives its acceleration.

To differentiate ${v}_{2}(t),$ we require the product rule. Let $g(t)=t$ and $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right).$ Then

$$
{g}^{′}(t)=1,\,{h}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right).
$$

We used the chain rule to calculate ${h}^{′}(t).$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2}(t) & ={v}_{2}^{′}(t) \\  & ={g}^{′}(t)\cdot h(t)+g(t)\cdot {h}^{′}(t) \\  & =(1)(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right))+(t)(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

owners.title: Differentiating a General Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule

candidates.solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{4}⁡(u)+7,\,u=6x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)}\cdot 6 \\  & =\frac{1}{(6x-2)ln⁡(4)}\cdot 6 \\  & =\frac{6}{(6x-2)ln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{(3x-1)ln⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1} & =\frac{3}{(3x-1)ln⁡(4)}{|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{(3(1)-1)ln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{2ln⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

candidates.prompt: Given the function $y=2{x}^{3}-5{log}_{3}⁡x,$ the slope of the tangent line at $x=2$ is{{field-1}}.
candidates.solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-5{log}_{3}⁡x) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{3}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}-5\cdot \frac{1}{xln⁡3} \\  & =6{x}^{2}-\frac{5}{xln⁡3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(6{x}^{2}-\frac{5}{xln⁡3})|}_{x=2} \\  & =6(2)^{2}-\frac{5}{2ln⁡3} \\  & =24-\frac{5}{2ln⁡3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

candidates.prompt:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x=
$$

candidates.solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)} & =\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{(x+4)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x+2=A(x+4)+B(x-2).
$$

Plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-4)+2 & =A(-4+4)+B(-4-2) \\ -6 & =-6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)+2 & =A(2+4)+B(2-2) \\ 6 & =6A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|+C\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|{|}_{3}^{6} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(40)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\  & =ln\,\left(\frac{40}{7}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

candidates.prompt:

$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 16{x}^{2},\,2\le xy\le 5\}.$
candidates.solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 16,\,2\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{16}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡16-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{9}\cdot (125-8) \\  & =26\operatorname{ln}⁡4.\end{aligned}
$$

\{\begin{aligned}x=r\cos\theta \\ y=r\sin\theta\end{aligned}
$$

candidates.prompt:
Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$

$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+1+Y(s)=\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s}.
$$

The solution is $y(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\,\cdot \,($
{{field-1}}
$)-\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).$
candidates.solution:
Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+1+Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s}-1 \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-\pi s/2}\cdot \frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}-\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=1$, $B=-1$, and $C=0$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-\pi s/2}(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1})\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{\pi /2}(t)(1-cos\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})(1-cos\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

owners.title: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Not Given

candidates.prompt:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
y=\frac{2}{x},\,y=\frac{5}{x},\,x={y}^{2},\,x=4{y}^{2}
$$
candidates.solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
xy=2,\,xy=5,\,\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=1,\,\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=4
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=xy,\,v=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=xy$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=2\,⟹\,u=2 \\  & xy=5\,⟹\,u=5\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=4\,⟹\,v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/ff/ff8f8b6af1d1a81a0c7f40b29e92351431a45f67ebc057fd39acd2cd2280f48b.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$
